newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's opposition unites on fears of poll fraud.
newsitem.headline: Romania's opposition unites on fears of poll fraud.

text.p: Romania's fractious opposition on Monday declared a truce in squabbling and joined forces to prevent any election fraud by leftists in power since the fall of Communism in 1989.

Ten parties, led by the biggest groups challenging President Ion Iliescu and his Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), signed a pact designed to ensure that Sunday's presidential and parliamentary polls were free of cheating.
But it was clear the alliance was a tactical one with no promises for post-election talks on forming a government.

"This accord underscores our worry following the latest actions of the government and the ruling party which leave the impression that the elections could be tainted," Emil Constantinescu, Iliescu's main rival, told reporters.
The pact called for joint observers to oversee operations in 15,000 polling stations, recording and collating vote counts throughout the country of 23 million.
Romania's splintered opposition parties all seek an end to Iliescu's seven-year hold on power, but have lost time by training much of their fire on each other.
Temporary unity seems to have been forged by a widespread belief that the PDSR, trailing in the parliamentary vote, has stage-managed a series of dirty tricks.
Reporters uncovered a poll conducted by an institute linked to the PDSR in which questions were loaded to swing opinion against Constantinescu and former prime minister Petre Roman.

Tension built as Constantinescu's Democratic Convention and Roman's Social Democratic Union accused the prefect of Bucharest of appointing officials sympathetic to the ruling party to run polling stations. They demanded his resignation.

Opinion polls show Iliescu, elected twice since taking power in the 1989 revolution that toppled Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, leading 16 candidates with 36 percent support. But that is short of the 50 percent needed for first-round victory.
Constantinescu has 24 percent and Roman 21 percent. Iliescu's party holds down second place in most surveys for the parliamentary vote.
The campaign has been peppered by television clips focusing more on personal attacks on rivals than explanations of policy.
Opposition spots show Iliescu juxtaposed with Ceausescu. The ruling party's publicity portrays Constantinescu as a closet monarchist and all but calls Roman a criminal.
Bucharest's press has been quick to predict widespread fraud engineered by the ruling party.

"Huge electoral fraud plotted," read Monday's editorial by political analyst Ion Cristoiu in the daily Evenimentul Zilei. He said the PDSR still held control over state administration, television and even the Central Electoral Bureau.

"The transformation of state television into a publicity agent for Iliescu and the PDSR, fake telephone polls, the huge number of presidential candidates, including some illegally registered are only some PDSR dirty moves," Cristoiu wrote.

Newspapers have warned against a repeat of fraud instigated in Romania's first post-war election in 1946, when Communists overturned a victory by the National Peasants' Party, with the connivance of Soviet troops, and took power two years later.
"In 1946, the elections were altered through violence, killings and abuses committed by organised groups controlled by the Red Army," Radu Campeanu, a leading liberal, told Reuters.
"In 1996, the fraud seems to be more sophisticated and computerised."
